title: Adapter Pattern
tagline: Wrap an incompatible interface in a translator so existing code works with new third-party APIs without a single change to the caller.

sections.content:
Imagine you have spent months building an `OrderService` that depends on a `PaymentProcessor` interface with a clean `charge(amount, currency)` method. Everything works perfectly. Then your company signs a contract with a new payment provider whose SDK looks nothing like what you built: instead of `charge(amount, currency)` it expects `makePayment({ total: amount, curr: currency, idempotencyKey: uuid() })`. You cannot rewrite every call site — there are dozens. You definitely cannot modify the vendor SDK — you do not own it. And you cannot ask your PM to wait three weeks while you refactor the entire payment pipeline.

This is exactly the situation the **Adapter pattern** was invented to solve. It introduces a thin wrapper class — the adapter — that implements the interface your system already knows and loves, and internally translates each call into whatever format the incompatible dependency expects. Your `OrderService` never changes. The vendor SDK never changes. The adapter absorbs all the friction between them.

The Adapter is a **structural design pattern**, meaning it is about how objects are composed together to form larger structures — not about algorithms or communication protocols. It falls into the same GoF (Gang of Four) structural category as Decorator, Proxy, and Facade, but it is distinguished by its singular purpose: **interface translation with no added behaviour**.

This chapter covers every aspect you need to master the pattern in production: the four canonical participants, object vs. class adapters, the difference between Adapter and related patterns, how to keep adapters thin, TypeScript examples with real-world payment and HTTP clients, testability benefits, and an honest look at when an adapter is overkill. By the end you will recognise the pattern immediately in frameworks you already use — because it is everywhere.

sections.caption: The full picture: OrderService is isolated behind the PaymentProcessor interface. Each adapter implements that interface and wraps a different incompatible backend. Adding a third provider means adding a third adapter — zero changes to OrderService.

sections.title: The International Power Adapter
sections.content:
You buy a laptop in the United States. Its plug has two flat pins arranged side by side — that is its interface to the world. You fly to Europe, and every wall socket expects a completely different plug: round pins, different spacing, higher voltage. You cannot chisel the socket into a different shape; you do not own the building. You cannot redesign your laptop's plug; you do not own the factory.

So you buy a **travel adapter**. It has a European-socket-shaped opening on one side and a US-plug-shaped cavity on the other. The laptop has no idea anything changed — it still plugs into something that accepts its US pins. The wall socket has no idea anything changed — something with European round pins is inserted. The adapter is pure mechanical translation.

Software adapters work identically. Your existing code (the laptop) expects a specific interface. The third-party library (the European socket) offers a completely different one. The Adapter class (the travel adapter) sits between them, presenting the expected shape to your code while internally speaking the library's language. Neither side is modified. Neither side knows about the other. All the translation is contained in one small, dedicated class.

This also captures a key limitation: the travel adapter does not add features. It does not charge your laptop faster or regulate voltage (well, some do — but those are doing extra work beyond pure adaptation). A software adapter, ideally, should be equally feature-free: just translation, nothing more.

sections.title: The Four Participants
sections.content:
The Adapter pattern has exactly four participants. Understanding each precisely prevents the most common mistakes:

**1. Target Interface** is the contract that your existing client code already depends on. In a typed language it is literally an interface or abstract class. In JavaScript it is the expected method signature. Your system was designed against this contract. All existing call sites invoke methods on this interface. The goal of the Adapter pattern is to make sure this interface never needs to change just because you are adding a new backend.

**2. Client** is any code that talks to the Target Interface. `OrderService`, `CheckoutController`, your unit tests — anything that calls `processor.charge(...)` is a Client. The Client does not know that an Adapter exists. It just holds a reference to something that satisfies the Target Interface, and it calls methods on it.

**3. Adaptee** is the incompatible class you want to use. It could be a third-party payment SDK, a legacy in-house module written years ago by someone who has left the company, or an external microservice whose API does not match your domain model. The Adaptee has functionality you need, but its interface does not match the Target. You cannot (or should not) modify it.

**4. Adapter** is the class that bridges the gap. It **implements** the Target Interface (so the Client can use it without knowing anything is different) and **composes** the Adaptee (holds a reference to it and delegates calls to it after translating the parameters and return values). The Adapter is the only class that knows about both sides.

**The key relationship to memorise:** `Adapter implements Target` + `Adapter wraps Adaptee`. Everything else follows from these two structural choices.

sections.title: Object Adapter vs. Class Adapter
sections.content:
There are two structural variants of the Adapter pattern, and they differ in how the Adapter relates to the Adaptee:

**Object Adapter** uses **composition**: the Adapter class holds a reference to an instance of the Adaptee. This is the dominant variant in modern code, especially in languages like JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, and Go that do not support multiple inheritance. Composition is preferred for several strong reasons:
- You can swap the Adaptee at runtime (pass a different instance to the constructor)
- You can adapt an entire class hierarchy — not just the specific Adaptee subclass
- It is easier to test: inject a fake Adaptee in unit tests
- It avoids the fragile base-class problem inherent in deep inheritance

**Class Adapter** uses **inheritance from both Target and Adaptee simultaneously**. The Adapter extends the Adaptee (to gain its implementation) and implements the Target Interface (to satisfy the Client). This requires multiple inheritance, which is not available in JavaScript or TypeScript. Languages like C++ support it, but even there, composition is generally preferred.

In practice: **always reach for the Object Adapter (composition)** unless you have a very specific reason not to. The rest of this chapter focuses exclusively on Object Adapters.

**A subtle point about constructor injection:** the Adaptee can be passed in through the constructor (most flexible, supports testing), created inside the constructor (simpler but harder to test), or even lazy-initialised. Constructor injection is the cleanest approach because it makes the dependency explicit and easy to replace.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Notice that `OrderService` is entirely unchanged between the Stripe and PayPal scenarios — only the injected adapter differs. Each adapter is a thin translator: it maps parameter names, reorders arguments, and discards or maps the return value. No business logic lives in either adapter.

sections.title: Keeping Adapters Thin: The Single Responsibility Principle
sections.content:
The most common mistake when implementing adapters is **leaking business logic into them**. It is tempting, because the adapter is already touching both sides of the integration boundary. But an adapter that calculates discounts, applies loyalty points, or validates business rules is violating the Single Responsibility Principle. It has become simultaneously a translator and a service — two reasons to change.

A well-designed adapter should do exactly three things and nothing more:

**1. Parameter translation** — map from Target method signatures to Adaptee method signatures. This includes renaming parameters, restructuring objects, changing units (dollars to cents, for example, if the SDK requires integers), and reordering arguments.

**2. Return-value translation** — map the Adaptee's response back into the shape the Target interface promises. If the Target says `charge()` returns `void`, unwrap the SDK response and discard or log it. If it returns a `{ transactionId: string }`, extract that field from whatever the SDK returns.

**3. Error translation** — if the Adaptee throws `StripeCardError`, the adapter should catch it and re-throw a domain error (`PaymentDeclinedError`) that makes sense in your system. This keeps Stripe-specific error types from leaking through the interface boundary.

**Nothing else belongs in the adapter.** If you catch yourself writing `if (amount > 1000) applyBulkDiscount()` inside an adapter, extract that into a domain service that wraps the adapter. The layering should be: `Client → Domain Service → Adapter → Adaptee`, not `Client → Fat Adapter`.

flowchart TD

sections.caption: The adapter's internal flow: receive a call in the Target's language, translate parameters, call the Adaptee, translate the result or error back, and return. No business logic belongs at any of these steps.

sections.title: Adapters and Testability

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Two adapters of the same Logger interface: `WinstonAdapter` for production (translates to Winston's unusual API) and `InMemoryLogger` for tests (stores calls in arrays for assertions). The service never changes between environments. This is the Adapter pattern's testability dividend at work.

sections.title: Adapter vs. Facade vs. Decorator vs. Proxy
sections.content:
Because the Adapter involves wrapping another object, it is frequently confused with three other structural patterns. The distinctions are sharp and worth memorising:

**Adapter vs. Facade:** A Facade simplifies a complex subsystem by providing a single, high-level interface over multiple classes. It does not need to match any pre-existing interface — it invents a new one. An Adapter must match a specific pre-existing interface (the Target) so that existing clients can use the Adaptee without modification. *If you are inventing a new interface to simplify complexity, it is probably a Facade. If you are implementing an existing interface to make something incompatible compatible, it is an Adapter.*

**Adapter vs. Decorator:** A Decorator also wraps an object, but it implements the **same interface** as the wrapped object and adds behaviour (logging, caching, access control) without changing the interface. An Adapter wraps an object with a **different interface** and translates between them without adding behaviour. *If wrapper and wrapped object share an interface, and the wrapper adds features, it is a Decorator. If they have different interfaces, it is an Adapter.*

**Adapter vs. Proxy:** A Proxy also wraps an object and implements the same interface, but its purpose is to control access, add lazy loading, or provide a remote surrogate — not to translate interfaces. Like the Decorator, the Proxy implements the **same** interface as the object it wraps. *If the wrapper and wrapped have the same interface and the purpose is access control or indirection, it is a Proxy. If the interfaces differ, it is an Adapter.*

Quick test: ask yourself — does the wrapper implement the **same** interface as the wrapped object, or a **different** one? Same interface: Decorator or Proxy (distinguished by purpose). Different interface: Adapter.

sections.caption: Decision tree for choosing between the four most commonly confused structural patterns. The key question is always: same interface or different interface?

sections.title: The Adapter Pattern in Real Frameworks and Libraries
sections.content:
Once you know what an Adapter looks like, you see it everywhere in production software:

**ORMs (TypeORM, Sequelize, Prisma):** These are adapters at architectural scale. Your application code talks to a clean `Repository` or `Model` interface. The ORM internally translates those calls into raw SQL for the specific database dialect (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite). Switching databases means swapping the ORM adapter, not rewriting your business logic.

**Node.js stream adapters:** Node's `stream.Writable`, `stream.Readable`, and `stream.Transform` are adapter-friendly abstractions. Libraries provide adapters that make blob storage APIs, HTTP responses, and file descriptors all appear as the same streaming interface.

**React's `useRef` and DOM adapters:** The synthetic event system in React is an adapter: it wraps browser-native DOM events behind a normalised `SyntheticEvent` interface so the same React component code works across browsers with their inconsistent native event APIs.

**Axios interceptors and `fetch` wrappers:** Teams often write an `HttpClient` interface with a `get(url, options)` / `post(url, body, options)` contract, then write adapters for Axios, the native `fetch` API, or a test double. Switching HTTP libraries means only the adapter changes.

**Testing library `@testing-library/user-event`:** This library adapts complex user gesture sequences (click, type, tab) into the `userEvent` API — itself an adapter layer over raw DOM event dispatching.

**`Array.from()`:** JavaScript's `Array.from()` is a functional adapter. It takes any iterable or array-like object (Set, Map, NodeList, generator, string) and adapts it to a plain `Array`. The caller gets a standard array regardless of what was passed in.

**Express middleware adapters:** Third-party packages frequently ship as adapters between their library's API and Express's `(req, res, next)` middleware interface. `passport.initialize()`, for example, adapts Passport's authentication strategies to Express's request pipeline.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: This HttpClient adapter layer is a pattern used by many large React and Node.js codebases. AxiosAdapter and FetchAdapter allow switching HTTP libraries without touching any service code. FakeHttpClient gives tests full control over responses and lets you assert exactly what URLs were called and with what bodies — without a single network request.

sections.content: **Historical context:** The Adapter (also called Wrapper) pattern was formally catalogued in the 1994 Gang of Four book *Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software* by Gamma, Helm, Johnson, and Vlissides. It is one of the original 23 patterns and has remained continuously relevant because the underlying problem — integrating systems with incompatible interfaces — never goes away. Every generation of software developers rediscovers it independently before naming it. If you have ever written a class that wraps a third-party library to match your own method signatures, you have already implemented an adapter.

sections.title: When to Use the Adapter Pattern
sections.content:
Use the Adapter pattern when **all three** of the following conditions hold simultaneously:

**1. You have an existing interface that existing code depends on.** This could be an explicit TypeScript/Java interface, a documented API contract, or simply a method signature that appears in dozens of call sites. The point is that the interface is established and changing it would require widespread edits.

**2. You have a class or module with the functionality you need, but its interface does not match.** This is the Adaptee — a third-party SDK, a legacy module, an external service's API. It does what you need functionally, but it speaks a different API language.

**3. You cannot (or should not) modify either the client code or the Adaptee.** If you own both sides, the simpler solution is to align them directly. If you own the Adaptee but not the Target, you might add a compatibility method. Adapters become necessary when both sides are fixed constraints.

Common scenarios that almost always call for an Adapter:
- **Third-party SDK integration** — payment providers, email services, cloud storage, mapping APIs
- **Legacy system integration** — wrapping an old module behind a modern interface
- **Microservice integration** — adapting a service's response schema to your domain model
- **Test doubles** — creating fake implementations of external dependencies
- **Multi-provider support** — when you need to switch between providers (Stripe vs. PayPal) based on configuration
- **Gradual migration** — wrapping an old implementation behind a new interface while you migrate call sites one at a time

**When NOT to use the Adapter:** If you control both the client and the dependency, just align the interfaces directly — the adapter adds an extra class, an extra layer of indirection, and an extra file to maintain. If the interfaces are only slightly different (a single parameter rename), a one-line translation at the call site is cheaper than a full adapter class. Avoid adapters that contain significant business logic — that logic belongs in a service layer. Finally, do not chain adapters (`Client → Adapter1 → Adapter2 → Adaptee`) to avoid touching client code at the cost of an inscrutable translation chain; at that point, refactoring the target interface is a better investment.

**In the wild — quick reference:**
- **ORMs**: TypeORM, Sequelize, Prisma (adapters over raw database drivers)
- **HTTP**: Axios adapters, fetch wrappers, superagent
- **React**: Synthetic event system adapting browser events
- **Node.js**: Stream adapters (`stream.Writable`, `stream.Transform`)
- **JS builtins**: `Array.from()`, `Promise.resolve()`, `Object.entries()`
- **Testing**: Jest mocks, Sinon stubs, custom test doubles all follow the adapter shape
- **Cloud**: AWS SDK v2 → v3 migration wrappers, Firebase compat libraries

items: The **Adapter pattern** makes two incompatible interfaces work together by introducing a wrapper class that implements the Target Interface and internally delegates to the Adaptee — neither side is modified.
The four participants are **Client** (caller), **Target Interface** (what the client expects), **Adapter** (the translator), and **Adaptee** (the incompatible class being wrapped).

Always use an **Object Adapter** (composition) over a Class Adapter (multiple inheritance): `Adapter implements Target` + `Adapter wraps Adaptee`. Composition allows runtime swapping and easy testing.
Adapters should contain **translation only** — parameter mapping, return-value mapping, and error translation. Business logic belongs in a service layer, not the adapter.

The Adapter pattern dramatically improves **testability**: because clients depend on the Target Interface, any concrete class implementing that interface — including simple in-memory fakes — can be injected in tests, eliminating the need to hit real external services.

The key distinction from related patterns: **Decorator** adds behaviour with the same interface; **Proxy** controls access with the same interface; **Facade** simplifies a complex subsystem with a new interface; **Adapter** makes an incompatible interface compatible with an existing one.
The pattern is ubiquitous in production code: ORMs, HTTP clients, React's event system, stream adapters, and virtually every integration with a third-party SDK follows the Adapter structure.

quiz.question: What is the defining structural relationship of the Object Adapter pattern?
options: Adapter extends both Target and Adaptee via multiple inheritance
Adapter implements the Target Interface and wraps the Adaptee via composition
Adapter extends the Adaptee and the Client extends the Target
Adapter and Adaptee both implement the Target Interface independently
quiz.explanation: The Object Adapter implements the Target Interface (so the Client can use it polymorphically) and holds a reference to the Adaptee via composition (so it can delegate and translate calls). This is the canonical structure.

quiz.question: Your OrderService calls processor.charge(amount, currency). A new SDK requires makePayment({ total, curr }). Which participant is the new SDK?
options: Target Interface
Client
Adapter
Adaptee
quiz.explanation: The Adaptee is the incompatible class you want to use — it has the functionality you need but a different interface. The new SDK (makePayment) is the Adaptee. OrderService is the Client, PaymentProcessor is the Target Interface.

quiz.question: Why is an Object Adapter (composition) preferred over a Class Adapter (inheritance from Adaptee) in modern languages?
options: Object adapters execute faster because they avoid virtual dispatch
Class adapters cannot implement interfaces, only abstract classes
Composition allows swapping the Adaptee at runtime and supports the entire Adaptee class hierarchy, not just one subclass
JavaScript garbage-collects composed objects faster than inherited ones
quiz.explanation: Composition decouples the Adapter from a specific Adaptee class — you can inject any conforming instance, including subclasses and fakes. Class adapters lock you to one concrete Adaptee class via inheritance and require multiple inheritance, which many languages do not support.

quiz.question: A developer adds discount calculation logic inside a StripeAdapter. What principle does this violate?
options: Open/Closed Principle — adapters must be closed to modification
Single Responsibility Principle — adapters should only translate, not contain business logic
Liskov Substitution Principle — adapters must be substitutable for the Target
Interface Segregation Principle — adapters must implement all interface methods
quiz.explanation: Adapters have one responsibility: translate between interfaces. Adding discount logic gives the adapter two reasons to change (translation changes AND business rule changes), violating the Single Responsibility Principle. Business logic belongs in a service layer.

quiz.question: You write a class that wraps a complex subsystem of 12 classes behind a single simplified interface you invented — there is no pre-existing interface to match. Which pattern is this?
options: Adapter
Decorator
Facade
Proxy
quiz.explanation: A Facade provides a simplified interface over a complex subsystem. Unlike the Adapter, it invents a new interface rather than matching a pre-existing one. The Adapter must implement a specific interface that existing clients already depend on.

quiz.question: How does the Adapter pattern improve unit testability of OrderService?
options: It auto-generates mock classes at compile time
It eliminates the need for dependency injection
Because OrderService depends on an interface, a simple FakePaymentProcessor can be injected in tests without hitting real payment APIs
Adapters cache external calls so tests run against cached data
quiz.explanation: Since OrderService depends on the PaymentProcessor interface (not a concrete Stripe class), any class implementing that interface — including a simple in-memory fake — can be injected. Tests get full control without network calls, credentials, or test accounts.

quiz.question: A Decorator and an Adapter both wrap an object. What is the clearest structural distinction between them?
options: Decorators use inheritance; Adapters use composition
A Decorator implements the same interface as the wrapped object; an Adapter implements a different interface
Adapters add new methods; Decorators remove methods
Decorators are only used for logging; Adapters are only used for payment systems
quiz.explanation: A Decorator wraps an object and implements the same interface, adding behaviour. An Adapter wraps an object with a different interface, translating between them. The interface relationship (same vs different) is the key structural distinction.

quiz.question: When should you NOT use the Adapter pattern?
options: When integrating a third-party SDK whose API differs from your domain model
When writing a fake implementation for unit tests
When you own both sides of the interface and can align them directly
When supporting multiple payment providers behind a single interface
quiz.explanation: If you control both the client code and the dependency, the simpler solution is to align the interfaces directly. An unnecessary adapter adds a class, a layer of indirection, and maintenance overhead without benefit.

quiz.question: Which of the following real-world examples best illustrates the Adapter pattern?
options: A Redux store that centralises all application state
An ORM that wraps raw database driver calls behind a clean model interface
A React component that uses useState for local form state
A binary search algorithm that runs in O(log n)
quiz.explanation: An ORM (TypeORM, Sequelize, Prisma) implements a clean model interface that your code depends on, while internally translating calls to raw SQL for the specific database driver — exactly the Adapter structure: Target Interface + Adapter + Adaptee.

quiz.question: Three things belong inside an adapter class. Which of these does NOT belong?
options: Parameter translation (renaming, restructuring, unit conversion)
Return-value translation (mapping SDK response to domain type)
Loyalty point calculation based on order amount
Error translation (catching StripeCardError, re-throwing PaymentDeclinedError)
quiz.explanation: Adapters should only translate: parameters in, return values out, and errors across the boundary. Loyalty point calculation is business logic and belongs in a domain service layer, not the adapter.
